The Browns gave you a walk-off win yesterday — 13–10 over Baltimore and a share of first place — so the city starts the week in a fighting mood. Overnight, Ukraine launched more than 1,000 drones at Russia, setting St. Petersburg oil sites ablaze, while Washington argued over intelligence sharing and the Russia sanctions waiver. Solon woke up clear and frosty at 34°, but it's a sunny, dry day ahead with a high near 67°. Tonight in town: Solon Council votes on the park and trail notes, the Jonas Brothers play Rocket Arena, and the Cleveland Orchestra trio performs at Severance — both shows at 7:30.

weekBrief.text: It's a classic crisp fall week in Solon: dry and sunny almost every day, highs in the mid-to-upper 60s and chilly nights in the 30s — good weather for getting outside and for playoff baseball. The Guardians need two wins in Florida to reach the World Series, with a possible Game 7 Tuesday and the Series itself starting Friday. The Browns take their share of first place to Tennessee on Sunday, the Cavs open at Philadelphia on Thursday and play their home opener Saturday against Brooklyn, and Ohio State gets a bye to heal up at quarterback after Saturday's win at Indiana. Around town: trunk-or-treat Thursday in Solon, Heinen's clam bake Friday in Chagrin Falls, and Barack Obama campaigns in Cleveland on Saturday for the fall races. Grocery play of the week is still Giant Eagle's free-turkey deal — spend $350 by November 8 — and the baby countdown is very much on, so it's a good week to knock a few more checklist items off together.

Ukraine fires more than 1,000 drones at Russia, setting St. Petersburg oil sites ablaze
items.summary:
Ukraine launched one of its largest aerial attacks of the war on Sunday, sending more than 1,000 drones at targets across Russia. Fires broke out at an oil export terminal and an oil depot in St. Petersburg, and local officials said one person was killed and several others were wounded.

Russia's defense ministry said its forces destroyed 1,015 drones across 15 regions, Crimea and the Black Sea. Companies also confirmed hits or fires at a large retail logistics center and a technology firm's data center, showing the attack reached well beyond military targets.

The barrage landed in the middle of a growing argument between Kyiv and Washington. Ukraine's president said Russia had struck Ukrainian energy sites dozens of times in the past week, while the White House has criticized Kyiv's attacks on Russian oil infrastructure.

Watch whether the scale of this strike changes the sanctions and diplomacy debate in Washington this week.

items.title: France cleans up after protests turn violent, with a historic town hall burned in Limoges
items.summary:
France is assessing damage after a weekend of nationwide protest that began largely peacefully and ended with looting, fires and clashes in multiple cities. Officials put Saturday's turnout at roughly 550,000 people, including about 110,000 in Paris, and arrests have since risen past 2,000.

The worst single loss was in Limoges, where the city's 143-year-old town hall was set on fire and its spire collapsed. Protesters also entered city buildings in Marseille and Lille, and a tourism office was torched in Lyon. The interior minister said more than 600 police officers were injured.

The movement grew out of student-led anger over school conditions and the cost of living, and it has widened into a broader complaint that the government is not listening. President Emmanuel Macron condemned the violence in a televised address and promised prosecutions.

Mayors from the hardest-hit cities are meeting the prime minister, and the political question now is whether the government offers a policy response before the unrest builds again.

items.title: Rubio says U.S. intelligence sharing with Ukraine was never paused, contradicting Zelenskiy
items.summary:
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Monday that American intelligence sharing with Ukraine was never interrupted, directly contradicting what Ukraine's president told a Sunday news program. Volodymyr Zelenskiy had said the flow was briefly cut off and later restored.

Rubio, speaking during a visit to Uzbekistan, told reporters to ask Zelenskiy where the claim came from and said both sides should focus on ending the war. U.S. officials have also denied a related Ukrainian suggestion that Washington limited access to a SpaceX-built satellite system used for defense.

Ukraine depends on American intelligence to spot fast-moving Russian missiles aimed at its cities, so even a short gap would matter on the ground. Ukrainian officials have said some recent Russian strikes arrived without the usual warning.

The public disagreement is another sign of how strained the Washington-Kyiv relationship has become, even as the administration says it is trying to broker an end to the war.

items.title: China's economy grows 4.5% in the third quarter, a little faster than expected
items.summary:
China reported Monday that its economy expanded 4.5% from a year earlier in the third quarter, slightly ahead of the 4.4% forecast and up from 4.3% in the spring. Growth for the first nine months of the year sits at 4.6%, inside Beijing's full-year target range.

Factory output and retail sales both improved in September, while exports have stayed strong enough to push the trade surplus toward record territory. The soft spots remain familiar: investment fell sharply over the first nine months and spending on property dropped by about a fifth.

That split picture — strong factories and exports, cautious households — is why analysts describe a two-speed economy. It also means China is leaning harder on foreign buyers at a moment when trade friction with Europe is rising.

With the annual target still in reach, the numbers reduce pressure for a large new stimulus package, though targeted support for home buyers and local governments continues.

items.title: Pope Leo leads Sunday prayers in his first big public appearance since lung cancer surgery
items.summary:
Pope Leo XIV led the Sunday Angelus from the Apostolic Palace window on Sunday, his first major public appearance since surgery to remove a cancerous tumor from his right lung. Thousands in St. Peter's Square applauded as the 71-year-old spoke in a firm voice.

Leo had been released from Rome's Gemelli hospital on Saturday, four days after the operation. He thanked his doctors and everyone who prayed for him, and said the experience left him feeling closer to people who are living with illness.

His surgeon said the removed growth was an adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer, and described the recovery as going well. The doctor saw no clinical reason to cancel the pope's planned trip to Latin America in November.

Leo said he will resume his duties gradually. Watch for how full his schedule becomes over the next two weeks as a signal of how the recovery is really going.

items.title: Trump endorses Netanyahu nine days before Israel's election
items.summary:
President Donald Trump publicly endorsed Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Sunday, nine days before Israel's parliamentary election on October 27. In a social media post he called Netanyahu a great warrior and a key partner against Iran.

Reporting on the endorsement noted it is the first time a sitting American president has openly backed a candidate in an Israeli election. Trump also suggested the United States would have to do more of the work itself if Israel chose a different leader.

Netanyahu thanked Trump publicly and stressed that Washington is Israel's closest friend. Polls cited in the reporting suggest Netanyahu's coalition may struggle to reach the 61 seats needed for a majority, which is what makes outside support politically valuable.

The endorsement ties the election outcome more closely to Washington. Whatever coalition emerges in Jerusalem will shape the next phase of U.S. policy toward Iran and the region.

items.title: Trump defends easing Russia sanctions as anger grows in Congress
items.summary:
President Trump is defending his decision to waive a new package of Russia sanctions, a move that drew rare public criticism from lawmakers in both parties over the weekend. Several Republicans called the waiver a concession that rewards Moscow while the war in Ukraine continues.

The White House argues that enforcing the sanctions now would get in the way of talks aimed at a durable peace deal. Trump has also pointed to energy prices, saying Russia is doing little to help Iran and that he wants to keep it that way.

Critics answer that earlier concessions were followed by more Russian attacks, not restraint. Ukraine's president has warned that siding with Moscow would be a historic mistake and has urged Trump to reverse course.

Congress is in recess until after the November elections, which limits how quickly lawmakers could try to override the waiver even if the votes existed.

items.title: Putin floats a three-way summit with Trump and Xi to decide Ukraine's future
items.summary:
Russian President Vladimir Putin has proposed a meeting next month with President Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping to discuss ending the war in Ukraine, according to people familiar with the discussions reported by The Wall Street Journal. Ukraine would not be at the table.

The idea reportedly came up in an October 9 phone call between Putin and Trump — the same call that produced a deal for the U.S. to buy Russian diesel. A Kremlin spokesman confirmed talks about a possible meeting but said there is no clear agreement on timing or agenda.

A senior U.S. official said Trump has not agreed to the summit, though he could be open to it given his long-standing promise to settle the war. One possible venue discussed is the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific summit in Shenzhen on November 18–19.

A three-way meeting without Kyiv would alarm European governments, because it suggests the war's outcome could be negotiated by major powers over Ukraine's head.

items.title: Ahead of the midterms, voters put the economy and cost of living far ahead of every other issue
items.summary:
A new AP-NORC survey of voters finds the economy and the cost of living dominating the final stretch before the November 3 midterms: 85% call the economy a major issue and 84% say the same about living costs. About half of voters are pessimistic about the future of both parties — and about democracy itself.

Overall, 36% of voters approve of President Trump's job performance while 64% disapprove. His strongest issue in the poll is crime, at 45% approval, while roughly three-quarters disapprove of his handling of the economy and four in five disapprove on the cost of living.

Asked who should control Congress, 47% favor Democrats in the House and 46% in the Senate, compared with 38% preferring Republicans in each chamber. Fifteen percent are unsure, with independents the most undecided.

The poll of 1,119 adults was conducted October 8–12. It is a snapshot, not a prediction — turnout in the next two weeks will decide whether these numbers turn into seats.

items.title: Most Americans blame Trump's policies for high prices, an earlier AP-NORC poll finds
items.summary:
A separate AP-NORC poll released earlier this month found deep frustration with prices: only 17% of adults approved of the president's handling of the cost of living and 26% approved of his handling of the economy overall, both new lows in that survey series.

A majority — 65% — said Trump's policies, rather than forces outside his control, are responsible for persistently high costs. Respondents pointed to tariffs and to continued unhappiness with the war with Iran as part of that judgment.

The interviews included voters from the president's own party who said they had expected everyday costs to improve by now and have not seen it. That kind of erosion among sympathetic voters is what campaigns watch most closely in October.

Together with the newer voter survey, the picture heading into the midterms is consistent: prices are the issue, and the president's numbers on prices are his weakest ground.

items.title: The White House press secretary job is open again — and George Santos has volunteered
items.summary:
White House press secretary Katie Zacharia is transitioning out of the job after five days, a tenure reported as the shortest in the role's history, after the president told reporters he had advised her to reconsider her position.

Into that vacancy stepped an unlikely volunteer: former Rep. George Santos, who posted on X that he is not technically looking for a job but would jump to serve as press secretary in a heartbeat. A widely shared satirical post claiming he had already been appointed was false — no such announcement has been made.

Zacharia's brief run drew heavy scrutiny, including questions about her credentials and a first briefing that lasted under 15 minutes with questions from only three reporters.

There is no word yet on a successor. Whoever takes the podium will inherit a midterm-season communications job with very little runway.

items.title: The AI stock selloff spreads to Asia as investors question the cost of the buildout
items.summary:
Technology shares linked to artificial intelligence fell across Asia on Monday, extending a Wall Street slide driven by a simple question: who pays for all of this? Japan's Nikkei dropped early in the session, with Taiwan and South Korea also weaker at points.

Asia sits in the middle of the AI supply chain — Japan makes chip equipment, Taiwan makes advanced semiconductors, and South Korea supplies memory — so doubts about American data-center spending travel fast. In Japan, several equipment and materials names fell around 5% in early trading.

The concern is not that demand for AI has vanished. It is that the infrastructure is being built with borrowed money, and borrowing costs have risen, which makes the eventual payoff harder to reach.

Earnings from major tech companies this week are the next test. Strong results could calm the financing fears; cautious spending guidance would likely deepen them.

items.title: U.S. stock futures bounce Monday as AI shares recover and oil falls
items.summary:
American stock futures rose early Monday as buyers stepped back into AI-linked shares after the market's worst week since late June. CoreWeave, Broadcom and Nvidia all gained in premarket trading, and Intel rose after an analyst upgrade.

Two things outside tech helped the mood: oil prices fell about 1.8% after the Russia sanctions waiver, and the benchmark 10-year Treasury yield eased. Cheaper energy and slightly lower borrowing costs are exactly the combination rattled investors wanted to see.

The calendar is now the story. Meta reports this week, Tesla follows on Wednesday, and SpaceX is scheduled to release results Tuesday, alongside Netflix, General Motors and GE Aerospace.

A one-morning bounce after a bad week is not a trend. This week's earnings will show whether companies are still spending freely on AI — and whether investors still applaud them for it.

items.title: The Fed's new headache: the AI boom itself may be keeping inflation up
items.summary:
A Reuters analysis published Monday argues that the artificial intelligence boom has become a genuine problem for the Federal Reserve — the flood of spending on data centers, chips and power is adding demand to the economy long before AI delivers productivity gains that would push prices down.

Central bankers gathering in Bangkok last week described the pattern openly: investment arrives first, benefits later. The Fed's chair called it a shock that hits the demand side before the supply side, and warned the transition could be bumpy.

That leaves the burden of tighter policy falling unevenly. Housing and ordinary businesses that borrow at today's rates feel the squeeze, while the biggest AI builders keep spending almost regardless of the rate.

Some strategists see paths for inflation to cool anyway — cheaper oil if the Iran war eases, or a slower data-center buildout as local opposition grows — but none of them are painless or quick.

items.title: Palantir drops 7.2% as the AI selloff hits software hardest
items.summary:
Palantir shares fell 7.2% in the session covered by Monday's market reporting, closing at $186.03 after opening above $201. Trading volume ran well above average, a sign the selling was broad rather than a few large orders.

The drop was much steeper than the wider market's: the Nasdaq fell 2.15% and the S&P 500 lost 1.09% in the same session, with Oracle, Microsoft and Nvidia also down. Palantir had set a record high only shortly before, leaving it exposed to profit-taking.

Analysts tied the move to the same financing anxiety hitting the whole AI complex — rising bond yields at data-center builders revived doubts about how the infrastructure boom gets paid for, and expensive software names took the sharpest losses.

After the fall, the stock still sits well above its 52-week low but more than 12% below its high. That gap is the week's argument in one number: enthusiasm is intact, but it is no longer unconditional.

items.title: SpaceX's cargo Dragon delivered the space station's final new solar arrays
items.summary:
NASA's latest cargo run to the International Space Station carried a milestone in its trunk: the fourth and final pair of roll-out solar arrays meant to boost the station's power supply. The uncrewed Dragon launched October 13 from Cape Canaveral with more than 6,300 pounds of supplies and science.

The spacecraft docked autonomously with the Harmony module on October 15. Six matching array wings are already deployed on the station; this last pair is scheduled for installation during spacewalks later this fall.

The cargo was not all hardware. Experiments aboard include work on making artificial retinas in microgravity, growing three-dimensional heart-tissue models, studying glass formation and growing brain organoids for disease research.

NASA describes the array installation as the final step in upgrading the station's power system — an investment in a laboratory that is also being prepared, eventually, for a controlled end of mission.

items.title: The federal deficit hit $1.99 trillion in fiscal 2026, the largest in five years
items.summary:
The Treasury reported Friday that the federal budget deficit rose to $1.99 trillion for the fiscal year that ended September 30 — up from $1.78 trillion the year before and the largest shortfall since the pandemic-spending year of 2021.

Both sides of the ledger set records: the government took in $5.40 trillion and spent $7.40 trillion. The single fastest-growing burden is the interest bill itself, which reached a record $1.36 trillion and now trails only Social Security and the big health programs.

One surprise driver was tariffs — in reverse. After a Supreme Court ruling struck down a large share of the new tariffs, the government paid out about $145 billion in refunds, cutting net tariff income by 11%.

Total federal debt passed $40 trillion about two months ago. The deficit equaled roughly 6.2% of the economy, about double what analysts usually describe as a sustainable level.

items.title: Guam begins cleanup after Super Typhoon Champi, with federal emergency aid approved
items.summary:
Super Typhoon Champi passed about ten miles south of Guam early Sunday at Category 4 strength, knocking out power to roughly half the island and closing airports, harbors and some health facilities. It has since moved into the Philippine Sea and away from land.

President Trump approved emergency declarations for Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands, clearing FEMA to coordinate federal help. Officials warned that relief supplies could take three to five days to reach the islands.

This is the third powerful typhoon to hit the Marianas this year, after storms in April and July — and some families were still living in temporary shelter from those earlier hits, which makes this recovery harder than the wind speeds alone suggest.

Damage assessments are still under way. The declarations can expand if the territories request more categories of assistance and the assessments support them.

items.title: Shoppers are getting uneasy about AI setting the prices they pay
items.summary:
American consumers are pushing back on a quiet change in how prices get set: digital shelf tags replacing paper ones, and AI tools that help chains decide what to charge based on how customers are predicted to respond.

Shoppers are used to prices moving for flights, hotels and rides. The anxiety starts when the same logic reaches groceries and burgers — especially the fear, fed by social media, that two people might be charged differently for the same item based on their personal data.

Large retailers and restaurant chains say critics misunderstand the tools, which they describe as ways to manage promotions and costs rather than charge individuals differently. Lawmakers and regulators are not waiting to find out — proposals to limit the use of personal data in pricing are already moving.

For households, the practical takeaway is simpler: the price on the shelf is becoming less fixed than it used to be, and the rules for that are being written right now.

items.title: A service member dies after a rappelling fall before a college football game in San Antonio
items.summary:
A military service member died after falling while rappelling from the ceiling to midfield before the University of Texas at San Antonio's annual Salute to Armed Forces and Veterans game against Navy on Saturday.

Nellis Air Force Base said the service member was assigned to the 6th Combat Training Squadron, Detachment 2. He was taken to a local hospital, where he later died, with fans and a band already in the stadium.

Demonstrations like the pregame rappel are a familiar part of military appreciation games, which is part of why the accident has drawn wide attention — it happened during a ceremonial moment, in front of a crowd, rather than in training out of public view.

An investigation is under way into what led to the fall. The service has not released further detail about the failure point.
items.source: Associated Press via Rapid City Post

items.title: 'No Kings: Vote Early' rallies turn a protest movement into a turnout push
items.summary:
Demonstrators gathered in all 50 states and Washington, D.C. on Saturday for the latest No Kings day of action — this one explicitly built around voting. Organizers called it 'No Kings: Vote Early' and aimed the crowds at the November 3 midterms, seventeen days out.

Earlier No Kings events focused on opposing the administration's use of executive power. Saturday's version kept those themes — voting rights, immigration enforcement and democratic institutions — but added practical voter help: checking registrations and making plans to cast ballots early where states allow it.

Organizers announced more than 3,000 events nationwide. The White House dismissed the effort as a Democratic turnout operation, which in a sense confirmed the strategy: both parties now treat early voting as a decisive battleground.

Early voting windows are opening state by state this week, including in Ohio, so the rallies' message has a short shelf life — and a clear deadline.

items.title: Guardians face elimination tonight in ALCS Game 6 at Tampa Bay
items.summary:
The Guardians' season is on the line tonight. Tampa Bay won Game 5 in Cleveland on Sunday, 3–1, behind seven strong innings from Drew Rasmussen, and now leads the best-of-seven ALCS three games to two.

Game 6 is tonight at 8 p.m. ET at Tropicana Field. Freddy Peralta starts for the Rays — he has thrown 6⅔ scoreless innings in this series — while Cleveland had not named a starter, and manager Stephen Vogt ruled out ace Gavin Williams on short rest, pointing to an opener instead.

Cleveland has done this before: it came back from a 2–0 hole in the Division Series against Chicago. But the math is unforgiving now — two road wins in two nights, or the season ends.

If the Guardians force it, Game 7 is Tuesday night, also in Florida. The World Series starts Friday against Milwaukee, the National League champion.

items.title: Browns beat the Ravens 13–10 on a walk-off field goal and grab a share of first place
items.summary:
Cleveland's defense carried the day on Sunday. Baltimore scored ten points on its first two possessions and nothing after, and the Browns rallied from a 10–0 halftime deficit to win 13–10 at Huntington Bank Field.

The turning point was Carson Schwesinger's forced fumble on Derrick Henry early in the fourth quarter, recovered at the Baltimore 35 and converted into the tying touchdown. In the final seconds, Deshaun Watson hit Jerry Jeudy for 33 yards, and Andre Szmyt kicked the winner as time expired — after an offside flag wiped out a block on his first attempt.

The win moves Cleveland to 4–2, tied with Baltimore and Pittsburgh atop the AFC North. Watson finished 16-of-26 for 164 yards, and Henry was held to 58 rushing yards.

Next up is a trip to Tennessee on Sunday, October 25. Enjoy first place this week — the division has three teams in it.

items.title: Ohio State edges Indiana 19–15, ends the Hoosiers' 22-game win streak — but loses its quarterback
items.summary:
Ohio State won the weekend's biggest college game on Saturday, beating Indiana 19–15 in Bloomington in a top-five matchup. The Buckeyes are now 6–1 and unbeaten in Big Ten play, and Indiana's 22-game winning streak — the longest in the country — is over.

The finish was inches close: Indiana's potential go-ahead touchdown catch in the final minute was ruled out of bounds by a foot on the line, and Ohio State ran out the clock. Jeremiah Smith caught a touchdown and Bo Jackson scored on a fourth-down catch late in the first half.

The cost was high. Quarterback Julian Sayin, who threw for 235 yards and two scores, left in the fourth quarter with a shoulder injury and is expected to miss multiple weeks. Backup Luke Fahey finished the game.

Ohio State has a bye to sort out the quarterback situation, then travels to USC on October 31. The Buckeyes also moved up to No. 3 in the AP poll.

items.title: Cleveland-Cliffs posts a stronger third quarter and guides higher for the end of the year
items.summary:
Cleveland-based steelmaker Cleveland-Cliffs reported third-quarter results this morning: revenue of $5.45 billion on steel shipments of about 4.15 million tons, at an average selling price of $1,177 per ton. The company held $3.2 billion in liquidity at the end of September.

The product mix tells the local story — hot-rolled steel was the largest share, followed by coated products, much of it bound for the auto industry that anchors manufacturing across northern Ohio. About 25,000 people work for Cliffs across the U.S. and Canada.

Management expects a better fourth quarter, guiding to roughly $715 million in adjusted earnings before the listed deductions, and said 2027 could exceed $4 billion on new contract pricing.

Cliffs executives walk analysts through the numbers on a call this morning at 8:30 a.m. ET. For a region wired into steel and autos, this is one of the bellwether reports of the fall.

items.title: Cleveland wants to extend its pause on new data centers into early 2027
items.summary:
Cleveland City Council is moving to extend the city's temporary pause on new standalone data centers until January 29, 2027. The current three-month moratorium was set to expire October 20.

The pause grew out of a council working group and three town halls, where residents raised questions about zoning, the power grid and water use. Those are not abstract concerns in Ohio: the state already has dozens of operating data centers and far more planned, most of the growth concentrated around Columbus.

Cleveland is not alone — one tracking count put the number of local data-center moratoriums statewide at 125 as of September. Communities are using the breathing room to write permanent rules instead of approving projects one at a time.

The extension heads to the Finance Committee next, then to the full council. Whatever rules come out of it will shape where the AI building boom is — and is not — welcome inside city limits.

items.title: Solon Council votes tonight on $13.2 million in park and trail notes
items.summary:
Tonight's Solon City Council meeting is the decision point for two borrowing ordinances that have been working through readings this month: $7.2 million in notes for Solon Community Park and $6 million for the Norfolk Southern Headwaters Connector Trail.

Both measures got their second reading on October 5, and tonight is the meeting where they become actionable — and the last scheduled chance for residents to comment before a vote. Council earlier slowed the combined package down, holding it in September to take more time.

The park money follows the Community Park's reopening and fall festival earlier this month, while the trail notes would advance a connector project residents have watched for several seasons.

Also on residents' minds tonight: three charter amendments headed to the November ballot. If you care about either the borrowing or the amendments, tonight at City Hall is the night to say so.
